domain_label: Turlock Home & Contractor Trades — Market, Demand & Saturation Economics
purpose: A method for sizing and reading the Turlock independent home-and-contractor-trades market: quantifying the demand drivers (the ~73k resident base and its aging 1950s-1990s housing stock, the light-commercial and ag/food-facility account base, and property-manager/multi-family turns), explaining why the sector holds roughly 22 visible firms via a two-speed licensing/skilled-labor barrier, accounting for the Modesto leakage that caps the count, separating crowded easy-entry segments from thin licensed-trade white-space, and expressing all revenue, margin and market-size figures strictly as labeled benchmark estimates (industry benchmark per truck/tech/employee x an observable size signal) rather than as stated facts for any named business such as Saunders, Johnson Plumbing, or Applied Electrical Services.
assumptions: no per-business revenue dataset is supplied; every dollar figure is a labeled benchmark estimate (benchmark per truck/tech/employee x an observable size signal), never an actual reported figure for any named business

the universe is the 22 verified Turlock independent home-and-trades firms in businesses.json (chains, Modesto-headquartered firms, and big-box installed-services excluded), as of the 2026-06-30 snapshot
city/county/state figures (population, income, household count, CSLB licensing rules, the $25,000 bond, permit and fee amounts) are cited public facts or explicitly labeled derivations

sub-category revenue bands are published trade benchmarks (revenue per truck / per technician / per electrician / per employee / per crew) scaled by an observable Turlock size signal (years in business, residential-vs-commercial mix, showroom presence, fleet/crew language), tagged estimate-not-actual with a confidence level and a confirmation path
Modesto (~218k population, ~15 miles north) is the regional trade anchor whose supply houses, franchise/national players and big-box installed services cap Turlock's high-ticket and specialty ceiling

catalog coverage is a FLOOR not a ceiling: the cash-basis informal tail (solo handymen, unlicensed cleaners and mowers) is real and uncounted, so true operating density is higher than the catalog figure
exclusions: per-trade tooling, fleet, supply-house sourcing and dispatch operations — covered by the operations KB
per-trade unit-economics, cost-structure and labor-archetype go/no-go business-model detail — covered by the business-models KB
any claim of an actual, reported, or audited dollar revenue for a named business
chain, franchise, and Modesto-headquartered trade firms, and big-box (Home Depot/Lowe's) installed services, which are outside the independents-only catalog
individual bid pricing, marketing execution, or crew scheduling for a specific operator
source_description: labeled benchmark estimates and cited public facts for the Turlock independent home-and-contractor-trades market, grounded in the home_trades deep-dive (DEEPDIVE.md), its upstream market_saturation and supply_ops analyses, the reconciled brief, and the 22-business source dataset (businesses.json); demand sizing uses Census household counts and the aging-housing-stock signal, sub-category revenue bands use published per-truck/per-tech contractor benchmarks, and saturation/leakage reads use census population and national specialty-trade establishments-per-capita figures
source_citation: U.S. Census QuickFacts (Turlock ~72,919 mid-2025 pop, $82,995 median HH income, ~46% Hispanic); ACS-derived ~23-25k household count; CSU Stanislaus enrollment (~8,455 UG Fall 2024, renters not high-ticket trade buyers); CSLB / CA statute (C-10/C-20/C-36/C-15/C-27 classes, the $1,000 rule, $25,000 contractor bond, SB 216 -> SB 1455 WC deferral to 1/1/2028); published contractor benchmarks (ServiceTitan, Projul, Level, Pineido, NECA, Aspire, Jobber, TheJanitorialStore 2026); distributor universe (Ferguson, Hajoca, SiteOne, Ewing, Graybar, WAXIE); home_trades DEEPDIVE.md, market_saturation.md, supply_ops.md, reconciled.md, businesses.json

competency_questions.question: What are the demand drivers that generate Turlock's home-trades spending base, and how large is the homeowner pool as a labeled estimate?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DEMAND_BASE names the homeowner base, the light-commercial/ag-facility accounts, and the property-manager/multi-family turns; HOUSEHOLD_POOL gives the ~23-25k household count (73k / ~2.9 persons, medium confidence) as the homeowner demand base, tagged estimate-not-actual

competency_questions.question: How does the discretionary-vs-non-discretionary split shape demand and price sensitivity across the trades?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DEMAND_DISCRETION separates non-discretionary event-driven work (plumbing/HVAC/electrical) from recurring-contract (janitorial/landscape maintenance) and discretionary rate-sensitive work (flooring, landscape install), and ties each to its price sensitivity and out-of-pocket funding

competency_questions.question: How does Turlock's aging 1950s-1990s housing stock and hot-valley climate drive recurring replacement and emergency demand?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HOUSING_STOCK_DRIVER quantifies the core-era housing age and ties it to recurring repair/replacement (water heaters, panels, repipes, HVAC changeouts) plus the 100F+ summer cooling-failure surge

competency_questions.question: How is a per-sub-category benchmark revenue band built so it is an honest estimate and never a stated fact for a named business?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: BENCHMARK_REVENUE_BANDS states the benchmark-per-unit x size-signal method, gives the per-sub-category bands, and tags every band estimate-not-actual with confidence and a confirmation path

competency_questions.question: Why is a high gross-revenue band never to be read as high profit, and how thin are the net margins by trade?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: MARGIN_REALITY pairs each gross band with its net-margin reality (HVAC 5-12% net on high equipment COGS, janitorial labor 50-60% of revenue, landscape maintenance labor 40-50%) so high gross is never mistaken for high net

competency_questions.question: Why does Turlock sustain roughly 22 visible independent trade firms, and what forces set that equilibrium?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SATURATION_EQUILIBRIUM names the forces (demand ceiling, Modesto leakage, the two-speed licensing/skilled-labor barrier, and the invisible informal tail) and ties the ~22 visible count to them

competency_questions.question: How does the two-speed entry barrier sort the sector into crowded easy-entry vs thin licensed segments?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: TWO_SPEED_BARRIER explains why CSLB licensing + the $25k bond + skilled-labor scarcity keep electrical/HVAC/plumbing/flooring thin while near-zero-barrier janitorial and landscape maintenance crowd

competency_questions.question: What is the catalog density per 10k residents, why is it a FLOOR, and what is the plausible true density?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DENSITY_FLOOR gives the ~3.0 firms/10k catalog figure, explains it is a measurement floor, and states the plausible 5-8/10k true density once the cash-basis informal tail is counted, against the 15-25+/10k national benchmark

competency_questions.question: How does Modesto's proximity cap Turlock's count and specifically leak high-ticket and specialty work north?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: MODESTO_LEAKAGE explains the ~15-mile leak to a 3x-larger anchor with supply houses, franchise/national players and big-box installed services, plus the lead-aggregator and DIY leak channels

competency_questions.question: How does the per-sub-category saturation read split the sector into crowded, balanced and thin?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SUBCATEGORY_SATURATION_READS gives the per-sub-category catalog count vs a realistic read: landscaping 7 crowded, plumbing 6 moderately served, janitorial 3 crowded-with-tail, HVAC 2-primary thin-but-~4-functional, electrical 2 thinnest, flooring 2 thin

competency_questions.question: How do seasonality and the community/labor base concentrate demand and shape who enters?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SEASONALITY_AND_COMMUNITY names HVAC summer surge, landscape spring-fall, and the labor-rich Hispanic/Assyrian/Portuguese-Azorean/Punjabi base that feeds the crowded easy-entry tail and the informal cash-basis operators

competency_questions.question: Where is the defensible white-space, what cost/regulatory gate qualifies it, and how is a go/no-go entry verdict reached and refreshed?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: WHITESPACE_RANKING ranks openings (local electrical especially solar/EV/panel, commercial HVAC for the ag/food belt, premium water-wise landscape, succession-acquisition), REGULATORY_COST_GATE applies the CSLB/$25k-bond/WC gate, MARKET_GO_NOGO refuses adding a 9th commodity-mowing landscaper or 4th residential cleaner, and MARKET_REVIEW_LOOP defines the refresh triggers (SB 1455 WC landing, solar/EV demand, new ag plant, demographic refresh)

glossary.definition: The structural fact that one demand base produces a crowded easy-entry segment (janitorial, landscape maintenance — near-zero licensing, truck-and-mower capex) and a thin licensed segment (electrical, HVAC, plumbing, flooring — CSLB license, $25k bond, skilled-labor scarcity); this barrier sets the sector's internal shape.

The honest revenue-estimation method used throughout: take a published per-truck / per-technician / per-electrician / per-employee / per-crew trade benchmark and scale it by an observable Turlock size signal (years in business, residential-vs-commercial language, showroom presence, fleet/crew wording), yielding a band tagged estimate-not-actual with a confidence level; no figure is asserted for any named business.

Plumbing, HVAC and electrical work triggered by failure (a dead water heater, a failed AC in 100F July, a tripping panel), with low price sensitivity at the moment of failure, out-of-pocket funded, and largely recession-resistant — distinct from recurring-contract and discretionary rate-sensitive demand.

The 22 catalog firms / 73,000 residents x 10,000 ~= 3.0 firms per 10k is explicitly a measurement FLOOR capturing only web-present independents; adjusted for the cash-basis informal tail and Modesto firms serving Turlock, plausible true density is 5-8/10k against a 15-25+/10k national specialty-trade benchmark.

The capping effect of Modesto (~218k, ~15 miles north) hosting regional supply houses, franchise/national plumbing/HVAC brands and big-box installed services, so high-ticket and specialty jobs leak north and thin the Turlock-headquartered count; an estimate of cross-shopping behavior, not a measured leakage figure.

The HVAC primary count is 2 (Horizon, Saunders), but DeHart and Turlock Plumbing Heating & Air carry HVAC as a secondary line, so functional HVAC capacity is closer to ~4; the 'thin' label applies only to the headline primary count.

The misread in which a high gross-revenue band (e.g., HVAC install $1M-$3M) is mistaken for high profit; net margins are thin and trade-specific (HVAC 5-12%, janitorial 10-25% on 50-60% labor, landscape maintenance 10-20% on 40-50% labor), so every gross band must travel with its net caveat.

The uncounted cash-basis universe of solo handymen, unlicensed house-cleaners and mowers, deepened by Turlock's labor-rich Hispanic/Assyrian/Portuguese/Punjabi communities and in-language referral channels; it makes every 'thin' sub-category 'thin among cataloged firms' and pushes true density above the 3.0/10k floor.

An acquisition entry path implied by multi-generation incumbents (Saunders 1948, Johnson 1960, Lopez 30+ yr, ASAP 30+ yr) facing owner-age and succession risk; buying an established license-tied book of business sidesteps the skilled-labor and brand-tenure barriers that otherwise gate the licensed trades.

The CSLB licensing/bonding/insurance barrier that can override a demand-true opening: a license for any job where labor + materials >= $1,000, a $25,000 contractor bond (LLCs add a $100,000 worker bond), workers' comp (mandatory for C-20 HVAC regardless of employee status), EPA 608 for HVAC, and the SB 216 -> SB 1455 WC-for-all-licensees deferral to 1/1/2028.

nodes.definition: Catalog the three overlapping buyers that feed Turlock's home-trades spending: a ~72,919 resident homeowner base in roughly 23-25k households at a ~$82,995 median household income; a light-commercial and ag/food-facility account base (offices, schools, churches, medical, dairy/nut-processing/food-packing plants) that is the recurring-revenue backbone for janitorial, HVAC and electrical; and property managers / multi-family operators whose apartment turns drive move-out cleaning, flooring replacement and plumbing. These three buyers, not the resident count alone, set the demand the 22 firms share, and CSU Stanislaus (~8,455 UG) adds renters, not high-ticket trade buyers.

excluded: converting the base into a household pool count

pros.claim: Naming three overlapping buyers explains recurring commercial demand a homeowner count alone cannot
pros.example: multi-year janitorial and HVAC contracts on ag/food facilities are the revenue backbone for ASAP and Ultimate, invisible in a pure-residential read

cons.claim: Overlapping buyers risk double-counting demand if treated as independent pools
cons.example: a property manager who also owns a Turlock home counted twice inflates the apparent base

failure_modes: treating CSU enrollment as net-new trade demand rather than renters
ignoring the ag/food-facility commercial base because it does not appear in the resident census
acceptance_tests: the three buyer types are each named with a public-fact magnitude (resident pop, household count, commercial/ag-facility presence) and tagged with their source confidence, and CSU students are explicitly excluded as high-ticket buyers
revisit_triggers: a census or ACS demographic refresh
a major ag/food plant opens, closes, or changes headcount
a multi-family development changes the property-manager base

base.update_signal: a population, household, or commercial-account figure is refreshed

nodes.definition: Explain the sector's defining demand feature: work splits sharply by discretion, and price sensitivity follows. Plumbing, HVAC and electrical are non-discretionary, event-driven failures (dead water heater, failed AC in 100F July, tripping panel) with low price sensitivity at the moment of failure; janitorial and landscape maintenance are recurring-contract work, price-competitive on renewal; flooring and landscape install/design are discretionary and rate-sensitive, softening when interest rates and remodel budgets tighten. Unlike insurance-shielded sectors, most of this work is out-of-pocket (homeowner cash, financing, HELOC), so demand is more income- and rate-sensitive overall.

included: the three discretion tiers and their price sensitivity
the rate-sensitivity of discretionary install work
excluded: the housing-stock age driver (its own node)

pros.claim: Tiering demand by discretion explains why plumbing/HVAC/electrical resist recession while flooring softens with rates
pros.example: a tripping panel gets fixed regardless of rates, but a flooring remodel waits when HELOC costs rise

cons.claim: The discretion tiers blur at the edges, so a tier label can mislead on a mixed job
cons.example: a planned repipe is non-discretionary in cause but discretionary in timing, sitting between tiers

failure_modes: treating all trade demand as recession-proof because the emergency tier is
ignoring that out-of-pocket funding makes even non-discretionary work income-sensitive at the margin
acceptance_tests: each of the three discretion tiers is named with at least one trade and its price-sensitivity and funding (out-of-pocket vs insurance) is stated explicitly
revisit_triggers: an interest-rate move changes remodel/install demand
a shift in insurance vs out-of-pocket funding for a trade
a recession signal tests the non-discretionary tier

base.update_signal: a rate move or funding-mix shift changes demand sensitivity

nodes.definition: Isolate how Turlock's aging core housing stock (built 1950s-1990s) and hot-valley climate convert the resident base into recurring, non-discretionary replacement and emergency demand. Aging homes drive a steady stream of water-heater swaps, panel upgrades, repipes, and HVAC changeouts — the highest-margin repair work in the sector. The 100F+ summer drives a sharp emergency cooling-failure surge that amplifies HVAC and the HVAC-secondary plumbing firms (DeHart, Turlock Plumbing Heating & Air). This driver is the primary reason the licensed mechanical trades retain steady demand even as discretionary remodel work fluctuates with rates.

included: recurring replacement work (water heaters, panels, repipes, changeouts)
excluded: seasonality across all trades (its own node)

pros.claim: Tying housing age and climate to replacement demand explains steady mechanical-trade demand a flat resident count would miss
pros.example: an aging panel feeding rising solar/EV upgrade demand is why electrical is thin-but-rising, not declining

cons.claim: Housing-age demand is hard to size without a permit-volume dataset, so it is directional not quantified
cons.example: knowing the stock is aging does not say how many water-heater swaps per year without permit data

failure_modes: treating replacement demand as flat when climate and housing age make HVAC strongly seasonal
ignoring that rising solar/EV/panel demand layers new electrical load on the aging-stock baseline
acceptance_tests: the core housing-stock era is stated and tied to at least three recurring replacement work types plus the summer cooling-failure surge
revisit_triggers: a building-permit volume release for the city/county
a climate or extreme-heat shift changes the cooling surge
a solar/EV adoption release changes electrical replacement demand

base.update_signal: a permit-volume, climate, or solar/EV-adoption figure changes

nodes.definition: Size the homeowner demand base as a labeled estimate: ~72,919 residents / ~2.9 persons per household yields ~23-25k occupied households (medium confidence — a model-derived figure, not a count). This household count, plus the light-commercial/ag-facility account base and the property-manager turns, is the addressable demand the 22 firms share; it is explicitly an estimate, not a measured figure. The true addressable base is somewhat above the city household count because firms also draw from rural south Stanislaus County, a magnitude left UNKNOWN — which means the saturation read is, if anything, conservative on the demand side.

excluded: the density-per-10k saturation read (its own node)

pros.claim: A transparent population-over-persons-per-household method gives a defensible base without quoting any business
pros.example: stating ~23-25k as 73k / 2.9 lets a reader audit the estimate end to end

cons.claim: A city-only household count understates the true addressable base because rural-county draw is excluded
cons.example: rural south-Stanislaus homeowners served by Turlock firms are not in the 23-25k figure

failure_modes: presenting the ~23-25k as a measured figure rather than an estimate
capping demand at the city figure and ignoring the rural trade-area uplift
acceptance_tests: the household pool is stated as ~23-25k with the explicit population-over-persons-per-household derivation, a confidence level, and the UNKNOWN rural-uplift caveat, tagged estimate-not-actual
revisit_triggers: an ACS household-count refresh
a persons-per-household revision
a trade-area study quantifies the rural-county draw

base.update_signal: a household count or persons-per-household figure is refreshed

nodes.definition: Build the per-sub-category revenue bands that are the primary, most defensible revenue view, every one a labeled estimate (published per-truck/per-tech/per-electrician/per-employee/per-crew benchmark x an observable Turlock size signal), never an actual figure for a named business. Representative bands: plumbing solo/owner-op $300k-$500k and established multi-truck $800k-$2.5M; HVAC established multi-truck $1M-$3M and smaller $400k-$700k; electrical 1-3 electricians $300k-$600k and small commercial-capable $600k-$1.5M; flooring showroom+install $500k-$1.5M; landscaping solo/single-crew $80k-$250k and multi-crew $400k-$1.5M; janitorial owner-op residential-lean $75k-$200k and commercial-contract $250k-$900k. Bands are wide on purpose because unit counts are UNKNOWN, and Central Valley wage/ticket levels put true figures at the lower-middle.

excluded: the gross-vs-net margin pairing (its own node)

pros.claim: Per-sub-category bands anchored to published per-truck/per-tech benchmarks give a planning estimate without quoting any operator
pros.example: a plumbing band of $300k-$500k for a solo from $350k-$550k revenue/truck x one truck is auditable and business-agnostic

cons.claim: Bands rest on national benchmarks and unobserved unit counts, so any single firm can sit far outside its band
cons.example: a multi-truck Johnson Plumbing could exceed the solo top while a one-truck firm falls below it

failure_modes: attaching a band to a named business as if it were that business's revenue
stating a single point figure instead of a wide unit-count-UNKNOWN band
acceptance_tests: each sub-category has a revenue band derived as benchmark-per-unit x a stated size signal, tagged estimate-not-actual with a confidence and confirmation path, and the unit-count-is-UNKNOWN caveat is present
revisit_triggers: a published per-truck/per-tech benchmark source updates
an observable size signal (trucks, crews, electricians, showroom) is measured for a firm
CDTFA or licensing-board distribution data lands

base.update_signal: a benchmark source or measured size signal changes

nodes.definition: Correct the most common revenue misread: a high gross-revenue band is not high profit. Net margins are thin and trade-specific: HVAC nets only 5-12% because condensers/furnaces are a high-COGS equipment purchase; flooring 5-12% on special-order product; plumbing/electrical service 10-20% with labor at ~25-35% of revenue; landscape maintenance 10-20% but labor-dominant at 40-50% of revenue; janitorial 10-25% where labor IS the product at 50-60% of revenue. Labor burden adds ~25-40% on top of base wages (FICA, FUTA/SUTA, workers' comp, benefits), and emergency/after-hours repair (35-55% gross) materially exceeds install gross. Every gross band must travel with its net caveat so a $1M-$3M HVAC band is never read as $1M-$3M of profit.

included: the repair-vs-install gross gap and labor burden

pros.claim: Pairing every gross band with its net reality stops a reader concluding a high-revenue trade is high-profit
pros.example: showing HVAC nets 5-12% on a $1M-$3M gross exposes the high-COGS equipment drag

cons.claim: Net-margin figures are themselves benchmark estimates and vary widely by firm scale and mix
cons.example: a repair-heavy plumber nets above the band while an install-heavy one nets below it

failure_modes: quoting a gross band as if it were profit
ignoring that labor-dominant trades (janitorial, landscape maintenance) are most margin-sensitive to wage moves
acceptance_tests: each trade's gross band is paired with a net-margin range and the labor-as-percent-of-revenue figure, and the repair-vs-install gross gap is stated
revisit_triggers: a wage or workers-comp-rate move changes labor burden
a published contractor-margin benchmark updates
an equipment-cost shift moves HVAC/flooring COGS

base.update_signal: a wage, WC-rate, or equipment-cost figure changes

nodes.definition: Explain why Turlock sustains roughly 22 visible independent trade firms as an equilibrium set by four forces: (1) a demand ceiling (~73k residents in 23-25k households + a slow-growing commercial/ag-facility base, with no tourism and no daytime in-commuter inflation); (2) the two-speed licensing/skilled-labor barrier that sorts firms into crowded easy-entry vs thin licensed; (3) Modesto leakage that pulls high-ticket and specialty work north; and (4) an invisible cash-basis informal tail that makes 22 a visible FLOOR, not the true operating count. The count is held down primarily by demand ceiling + Modesto leakage; its internal shape is set by the licensing barrier; and the true density is higher once the informal tail is counted.

excluded: the two-speed barrier mechanism detail (its own node)
the Modesto mechanism detail (its own node)

pros.claim: Framing 22 as a visible-floor equilibrium of four forces resists both over-building and false-deficit conclusions
pros.example: it explains why a thin electrical count is white-space while a crowded landscaping count is not a deficit

cons.claim: An equilibrium framing can imply false stability when SB 1455 WC, solar/EV demand and succession are moving the forces
cons.example: treating 22 as fixed when the WC cost-shock could thin the smallest licensed operators

failure_modes: reading the 22 count as a deficit and recommending broad expansion
ignoring that the equilibrium is a visible floor with a real uncounted tail
acceptance_tests: all four forces are named and each is tied to the ~22-visible-count outcome, with the visible-floor-vs-true-count distinction stated explicitly
revisit_triggers: one of the four forces shifts materially (demand ceiling, licensing barrier, Modesto draw, or the informal tail)
the visible firm count moves away from ~22
the SB 1455 WC deferral lands and thins the licensed count

base.update_signal: one of the four equilibrium forces shifts

nodes.definition: Explain the barrier that sets the sector's internal shape: the same demand base produces a crowded easy-entry segment and a thin licensed segment because entry is two-speed. Licensed trades are gated hard — CSLB licensing (C-10 electrical, C-20 HVAC, C-36 plumbing, C-15 flooring), a $25,000 contractor bond, workers' comp, and the binding constraint of skilled journeyman/apprentice labor that cannot be conjured quickly — which is why electrical (2), HVAC (2 primary), plumbing (6) and flooring (2) are thin and concentrated. Janitorial (not CSLB-gated; city license + bond) and landscape maintenance (truck-and-mower capex) are barely gated, so a labor-rich community produces many small operators — which is why landscaping (7) and janitorial are the crowded sub-categories.

included: the hard-gated licensed trades and their classes
the skilled-labor scarcity as the binding constraint
excluded: the specific fee/bond figures applied as a verdict gate (REGULATORY_COST_GATE)
per-sub-category counts vs ceilings (its own node)

pros.claim: Naming the two-speed barrier explains the crowded-vs-thin split a single demand base would not predict
pros.example: the same 73k base yields 7 landscapers and 2 electricians because one is gated and the other is not

cons.claim: The barrier framing understates that some easy-entry firms (ASAP, Lopez) build durable moats via contract retention and tenure
cons.example: a 30-year janitorial firm is defensible despite near-zero entry barriers

failure_modes: treating skilled labor as a cost line rather than a hard supply constraint
assuming the easy-entry segments have no defensibility at all
acceptance_tests: the hard-gated licensed trades and the barely-gated easy-entry trades are each named with their CSLB class (or lack of one) and the skilled-labor scarcity is identified as the binding constraint
revisit_triggers: a CSLB licensing or bond rule changes
a skilled-labor supply shift (apprenticeship, migration)
a sub-category crosses from thin to crowded or vice versa

base.update_signal: a licensing rule or skilled-labor supply shift changes the barrier

nodes.definition: Read the saturation quantitatively as a FLOOR: 22 firms / 73,000 residents x 10,000 ~= 3.0 independent home-trades firms per 10k. This is explicitly a measurement floor capturing only identifiable web-present independents; adding solo handymen, cash-basis/informal operators (significant given the labor pool), and Modesto-based firms that service Turlock plausibly raises adjusted true density to 5-8/10k (low confidence). Nationally, specialty-trade contractors run on the order of 15-25+/10k when all trades and informal operators are counted, so Turlock's catalog-visible 3.0/10k is not saturated on paper — but that gap is mostly a measurement artifact layered on genuine Modesto leakage, not evidence of a wide-open market.

included: the 15-25+/10k national benchmark and the artifact-vs-leakage read
excluded: the per-sub-category saturation reads (its own node)
the Modesto leakage mechanism (its own node)

pros.claim: Stating density as a floor against a national benchmark prevents reading 3.0/10k as a wide-open market
pros.example: showing the gap is mostly measurement artifact + Modesto leakage stops a naive expand-everywhere conclusion

cons.claim: The true-density adjustment is low-confidence, so the 5-8/10k figure is itself an estimate of an invisible population
cons.example: without a cash-economy survey the informal-tail size is genuinely unknown

failure_modes: reading the 3.0/10k floor as the true count and concluding the market is under-served everywhere
comparing the catalog floor to the all-inclusive national benchmark without noting the definitional mismatch
acceptance_tests: the 3.0/10k catalog figure is derived and labeled a floor, the 5-8/10k true-density estimate and the 15-25+/10k national benchmark are stated, and the artifact-vs-leakage interpretation is given
revisit_triggers: the catalog firm count changes
a cash-economy or informal-operator survey lands
a national specialty-trade establishments-per-capita update

base.update_signal: the firm count or an informal-tail survey changes the density read

nodes.definition: Model the Modesto ceiling: Modesto (~218,000, three times Turlock's population, ~15 miles north) hosts the regional concentration of larger trade firms, supply houses, national/franchise players (Roto-Rooter-class drain brands, regional HVAC chains), and big-box installed services (Home Depot/Lowe's flooring, water heaters, HVAC). High-ticket and specialty jobs leak north, thinning the Turlock-headquartered count, and this leakage is the dominant cap alongside the demand ceiling. Additional leak channels: lead aggregators (Angi/Thumbtack/Yelp) that commoditize price, online/DIY product purchasing that pulls margin out of flooring and plumbing supply, and the informal/uncataloged operators within Turlock that pull the low end away from named firms. The leakage is an estimate of behavior, not a measured figure.

included: the Modesto anchor effect on high-ticket/specialty work
the lead-aggregator and DIY leak channels

pros.claim: Naming Modesto leakage explains the thin Turlock-headquartered count that demand math alone cannot
pros.example: high-ticket HVAC changeouts and specialty switchgear jobs leak north, capping local specialty depth

cons.claim: Leakage is inferred from proximity and scale, not measured, so its magnitude is uncertain
cons.example: without a cross-shop study the exact share of Turlock high-ticket spend going to Modesto is unknown

failure_modes: treating the leakage estimate as a measured figure
applying the high-ticket leak logic to non-discretionary emergency work that stays local by necessity
acceptance_tests: the Modesto anchor is quantified by population ratio and distance, tied to high-ticket/specialty leakage and at least two leak channels, and flagged as an estimate of cross-shopping behavior with its confirmation path
revisit_triggers: a Turlock-vs-Modesto cross-shop leakage study is done
Modesto's supply-house/franchise concentration expands or contracts
a big-box installed-services policy change shifts the leak

base.update_signal: Modesto cross-shop behavior or its trade concentration changes

nodes.definition: Give the per-sub-category saturation read by setting each catalog count against a realistic read for a 73k town: landscaping 7 — the single most-crowded, commodity-mowing race-to-the-bottom; plumbing 6 — moderately served, licensing + 24/7 emergency (PRO, Turlock Plumbing Co) + decades of brand (Johnson 1960) create defensible positions; janitorial 3 cataloged with a larger informal tail — commercial-contract (ASAP, Ultimate) sticky vs residential/move-out (Barbara's) churny; HVAC 2 primary (Horizon, Saunders 1948) but ~4 functional with the plumbing cross-sellers; electrical 2 (AEI, Frayer) — the thinnest licensed trade and clearest white-space on count; flooring 2 (Arrow, Turlock Floor Covering) — thin, with big-box and Modesto absorbing demand. Read every 'thin' as 'thin among cataloged firms.'

excluded: white-space ranking and the cost gate

pros.claim: A count-vs-read table makes each sub-category's crowding or thinness legible at a glance
pros.example: landscaping 7 reads as crowded while electrical 2 reads as the clearest white-space

cons.claim: Catalog counts undercount the informal tail, so a 'crowded' read can understate true crowding and a 'thin' read overstate scarcity
cons.example: landscaping is more crowded than 7 once unlicensed mowers are counted

failure_modes: reading a primary-category count as the full picture when HVAC secondaries shift it to ~4
treating a thin cataloged count as true scarcity when the informal tail fills it
acceptance_tests: each of the six sub-categories has a catalog count and a crowded/moderate/thin read consistent with the two-speed barrier and Modesto leakage, and the functional-vs-headline HVAC distinction is stated
revisit_triggers: a firm opens or closes in the catalog
a demographic or labor shift changes the informal tail
Modesto leakage for a sub-category is measured

base.update_signal: a sub-category count or its anchoring demand changes

nodes.definition: Account for the two demand-shaping forces an annual count averages away. Seasonality: HVAC is strongly seasonal (100F+ summer cooling surge); landscaping is spring-fall install/mow with winter cleanup/dormant pruning; plumbing/electrical are less seasonal, tied to housing age and emergencies; janitorial is non-seasonal recurring nights/weekends; flooring tracks remodel/real-estate cycles. Community/labor base: a labor-rich Hispanic (~46%, names like Lopez, Diaz & Flores, Capote), Assyrian (~20k), Portuguese/Azorean (~7%) and Punjabi/Sikh population feeds the crowded easy-entry tail via in-language referral channels that lower customer-acquisition cost — supporting more small firms per capita while simultaneously enlarging the uncounted informal tail and the ag/dairy-facility commercial account base.

included: the labor-rich community base and in-language referral channels
the link from community to the informal tail and ag-facility accounts

pros.claim: Surfacing seasonality and the community labor base explains both demand peaks and the crowded easy-entry shape
pros.example: an HVAC firm's summer surge and a Spanish-language-referral landscaper both shape the count a flat read misses

cons.claim: Community-share figures are directional community estimates, not Census-precise, so the labor-base read is qualitative
cons.example: the Assyrian ~20k figure is community-sourced, not a clean Census field

failure_modes: averaging a strongly seasonal HVAC firm into a flat annual band and mis-sizing working capital
treating the community labor base as raising the demand ceiling rather than enabling more sub-scale operators
acceptance_tests: each trade is tied to its seasonal profile and at least three heritage/labor communities are named as feeding the easy-entry tail and the ag-facility account base, with the informal-tail link stated
revisit_triggers: a climate or extreme-heat shift changes a seasonal peak
a demographic refresh changes the community labor base
an ag-facility account base change shifts commercial demand

base.update_signal: a seasonal peak or community-base figure changes

nodes.definition: Separate growing demand lanes from pressured ones using national trends overlaid on local fit. Growing: residential electrical tied to solar/EV/panel-upgrade adoption (the clearest local growth lane, rising on an aging-stock baseline); commercial HVAC for the ag/food-facility belt (recurring, high-ticket, defensible). Stable/non-discretionary: emergency plumbing and HVAC repair (event-driven, recession-resistant). Under pressure: commodity landscape maintenance (race-to-the-bottom pricing as supply is commoditized and shared) and undifferentiated residential cleaning (trivial entry, deep informal competition). Flooring tracks remodel/real-estate cycles and softens with rates. The growth lanes sit in the licensed trades where the moat protects the entrant; the pressured lanes sit in the easy-entry tail.

included: pressured easy-entry lanes (commodity mowing, residential cleaning)
excluded: white-space ranking and the cost gate (its own node)

pros.claim: Overlaying trajectory on local fit distinguishes a thin-but-growing licensed lane from a crowded-and-pressured easy-entry one
pros.example: electrical is thin by count yet growing on solar/EV, while landscape maintenance is crowded and price-pressured

cons.claim: Growth signals (solar/EV) are demand-side and can be absorbed by Modesto firms or solar installers, not just local electricians
cons.example: rising panel-upgrade demand may leak to Modesto solar installers rather than lift Turlock's two C-10 firms

failure_modes: treating commodity landscape maintenance as a growth lane because demand exists when pricing is a race to the bottom
assuming solar/EV growth automatically accrues to the thin local electrical count
acceptance_tests: growing, stable and pressured lanes are each named with their demand basis and tied to whether they sit in the licensed-moat or easy-entry segment
revisit_triggers: a solar/EV/panel adoption release
a national specialty-trade trend update
a local sub-category visibly gains or loses firms against the trend

base.update_signal: a solar/EV adoption or national-trend release shifts a trajectory

nodes.definition: Locate and rank the defensible white-space — openings where both demand and operations permit entry — and mark each viable only after the regulatory cost gate clears. Ranked: (1) local electrical capacity, especially solar/EV/panel upgrades (the best-supported headroom: thin count + rising non-discretionary demand, with the licensing/skilled-labor moat high enough to protect a well-run entrant); (2) commercial HVAC for the ag/food-facility belt (recurring, high-ticket, defensible); (3) premium/specialized landscape — water-wise/drought design, lighting, irrigation (the only defensible position above the commodity-mowing floor; Diaz & Flores' eco angle, Capote's concrete cross-sell); (4) succession-acquisition of a multi-generation incumbent (Saunders, Johnson, Lopez, ASAP) as an entry path that buys a license-tied book rather than building green-field.

included: the cost-gate qualifier and the succession path
excluded: the per-decision go/no-go verdict (its own node)

pros.claim: Ranking white-space by demand and feasibility together prevents recommending a demand-true but un-enterable trade
pros.example: local electrical ranks first because thin count, rising solar/EV demand, and a protecting moat all align

cons.claim: A ranked list can read as a recommendation to enter when each opening still needs an operator's own feasibility and licensing check
cons.example: commercial HVAC ranks high but a new entrant still needs a C-20 holder and EPA-608 techs

failure_modes: listing white-space on demand alone without the regulatory gate, so a licensed trade looks open when the CSLB/skilled-labor wall is high
ranking a succession-acquisition without flagging owner-age and book-transfer risk
acceptance_tests: at least four white-space openings are ranked, each with its demand basis and an explicit cost/regulatory-gate qualifier, and the succession-acquisition path is included
revisit_triggers: a white-space opening is entered locally
a demand or trend shift changes an opening's basis
a licensing/fee change moves the cost gate

base.update_signal: a white-space opening is entered or its demand/cost gate changes

nodes.definition: Define the regulatory/cost gate that can override a demand-true opening, the barrier the demand view alone misses. Licensed trades require a CSLB license for any job where labor + materials >= $1,000 (the '$1k rule') in the relevant class (C-10, C-20, C-36, C-15, C-27), a $25,000 contractor bond on file (LLCs add a $100,000 worker bond), workers' comp for any contractor with employees (C-20 HVAC cannot claim a WC exemption regardless of employee status), EPA Section 608 refrigerant certification for HVAC, and permits/inspection for panel upgrades, water heaters, repipes and changeouts. The near-term shock is the SB 216 -> SB 1455 deferral of WC-for-all-licensees to 1/1/2028, which when it lands raises the fixed-cost floor on the smallest licensed operators. These are cited public facts; the binding constraint is often licensing + skilled labor, not capital.

included: the $1k-rule license requirement and CSLB classes
the $25k bond and LLC $100k worker bond
WC (mandatory for C-20), EPA 608, and the SB 1455 WC deferral to 2028

pros.claim: Foregrounding the regulatory gate prevents a demand-true opening from being read as actually enterable
pros.example: local electrical looks open on demand until the C-10 license, $25k bond and skilled-labor wall are priced in

cons.claim: Fee and bond costs are knowable but the WC cost-shock timing and skilled-labor cost vary, so the gate is a range not a fixed cost
cons.example: the SB 1455 WC-for-all landing in 2028 is a near-term but not-yet-priced cost on the smallest operators

failure_modes: recommending a licensed-trade opening without pricing the CSLB/bond/WC/skilled-labor gate
treating the WC exemption as available to a C-20 HVAC operator when it is not
acceptance_tests: the $1k-rule license requirement, the $25k bond, WC (with the C-20 no-exemption note), EPA 608, and the SB 1455 WC-to-2028 deferral are each stated with their cited public basis and applied as an override on the relevant white-space openings
revisit_triggers: a CSLB or city/county fee schedule changes
the SB 1455 WC-for-all-licensees deferral lands or moves again
an EPA refrigerant rule changes HVAC entry cost

base.update_signal: a license, bond, WC, or refrigerant rule or fee changes

nodes.definition: Read the uncounted cash-basis universe that makes the catalog a floor: solo handymen, unlicensed house-cleaners and mowers operating below the web-visible threshold, deepened by Turlock's labor-rich Hispanic, Assyrian, Portuguese and Punjabi communities and their in-language, high-trust referral channels. This tail is concentrated in the easy-entry segments (landscaping, house-cleaning) precisely where the CSLB gate is weakest, so it pulls the low end of demand away from named firms and makes every 'thin' sub-category 'thin among cataloged firms.' It is the reason true density (5-8/10k) exceeds the 3.0/10k catalog floor, and it cannot be responsibly sized without a cash-economy survey — a flagged UNKNOWN, not a fillable gap.

excluded: the catalog density derivation (its own node)
the regulatory gate that licensed trades face

pros.claim: Naming the informal tail keeps every saturation read honest as a floor and prevents a false-scarcity conclusion
pros.example: reading landscaping as 'crowded among cataloged firms' acknowledges the deeper unlicensed-mower tail

cons.claim: The tail is by definition unobservable, so its size and effect are low-confidence estimates
cons.example: no dataset counts cash-basis cleaners, so the 5-8/10k true density rests on inference

failure_modes: filling the UNKNOWN tail size with a fabricated count
ignoring the tail and reading a thin cataloged count as true market scarcity
acceptance_tests: the informal tail is named, tied to the easy-entry segments where it concentrates, and flagged as the reason the catalog is a floor with an UNKNOWN true size requiring a cash-economy survey to confirm
revisit_triggers: a cash-economy or informal-operator survey lands
a licensing-enforcement change shifts operators in or out of the formal catalog
a demographic refresh changes the labor base feeding the tail

base.update_signal: an informal-operator survey or enforcement change updates the tail read

nodes.definition: Place Turlock's count in regional context: it sits in Modesto's gravitational shadow (~218k, ~15 miles north) with no offsetting tourism or daytime in-commuter base to inflate trade volume, unlike a Bay-Area-spillover commuter town. The clearest contextual reads are that high-ticket and specialty work leaks to Modesto's deeper supply-house and franchise concentration while non-discretionary emergency work stays local, and that the true addressable base extends above the 73k city figure into rural south Stanislaus County (an UNKNOWN uplift). This context is why the saturation read is conservative on demand and why the white-space sits in defensible licensed trades rather than in the commodity tail that the informal operators and Modesto both pressure.

included: Modesto's regional dominance and the no-tourism/no-commuter contrast
excluded: white-space ranking and the cost gate

pros.claim: Contextualizing against Modesto and the rural trade area places the 22 count in regional terms rather than in isolation
pros.example: no tourism or in-commuter base means resident + commercial demand is the whole ceiling, capped further by Modesto

cons.claim: The rural trade-area uplift is UNKNOWN, so the contextual demand ceiling is a range with an open upper bound
cons.example: without a trade-area study the rural-county share of demand is unquantified

failure_modes: comparing Turlock to a Bay-Area commuter town as if their trade demand structures matched
ignoring that rural-county draw makes the city-only ceiling conservative
acceptance_tests: Modesto's regional dominance is stated with population and distance, the no-tourism/no-commuter contrast and the high-ticket-leaks-vs-emergency-stays-local split are named, and the rural-county uplift is flagged UNKNOWN
revisit_triggers: a trade-area study quantifies the rural-county draw
Modesto's trade concentration shifts
a new commuter or employment pattern emerges in Turlock

base.update_signal: a trade-area or Modesto-concentration figure changes

nodes.definition: Read the sector's structural spine: it runs on two distinct economic engines, and almost every conclusion flows from that split. Engine A — licensed, event-driven mechanical trades (electrical, HVAC, plumbing) — carries real moats (CSLB license tied to an RMO, bonds, workers' comp, EPA-608, and skilled journeyman/apprentice labor that cannot be conjured quickly) and largely non-discretionary demand. Engine B — easy-entry, labor-is-the-product recurring services (janitorial, landscape maintenance) — has near-zero licensing barriers, thin shared supply chains, and low capex, with defensibility coming only from contract retention, not from any supply or capital moat. Moat strength on one side, saturation on the other, is the division that organizes the whole analysis.

included: the Engine-A moat trades vs Engine-B easy-entry split
moat sources (license, bond, WC, skilled labor) vs contract-retention defensibility

pros.claim: The two-engine split organizes every downstream read into a moat side and a saturation side
pros.example: it explains why electrical is white-space and landscaping is a price scrum from a single structural cut

cons.claim: The clean two-engine split blurs for cross-sell firms that straddle both (plumbing-primary with HVAC secondary)
cons.example: DeHart sits in Engine A on plumbing and HVAC but its drain-cleaning side is more commoditized

failure_modes: assuming Engine-B firms have no defensibility when contract retention is a real moat
treating a straddling cross-sell firm as purely one engine
acceptance_tests: both engines are named with their defining trades, Engine A's moat sources and Engine B's contract-retention-only defensibility are stated, and the moat-strength-vs-saturation framing is made explicit
revisit_triggers: a licensing change alters Engine A's moat
a contract-retention or labor-market shift alters Engine B's defensibility
a cross-sell firm changes its engine mix

base.update_signal: a moat source or contract-retention dynamic shifts

nodes.definition: Enforce the binding honesty discipline across every dollar figure: per-business revenue is not public for these privately held independents, so no dollar figure is ever stated as an actual reported figure for a named business such as Saunders, Johnson Plumbing, or Applied Electrical Services. Every sub-category dollar band is a labeled benchmark estimate (published per-truck/per-tech benchmark x an observable size signal) tagged estimate-not-actual with a confidence level and a confirmation path; every high-gross band is paired with its thin-net-margin caveat; city/county/state figures (population, income, the $25k bond, CSLB rules) are cited public facts or labeled derivations; supplier-to-named-business links are representative inference unless a cited source states otherwise; and coverage is reported as a FLOOR not a ceiling. This guardrail governs how all sizing and band nodes may be expressed.

included: the public-fact-vs-derivation distinction and the coverage-floor rule

pros.claim: A single explicit guardrail keeps every downstream number honest and auditable
pros.example: tagging every sub-category band and the density figure estimate-not-actual prevents any figure being read as audited fact about a named firm

cons.claim: Heavy labeling can make the analysis read as hedged and lower its perceived usefulness
cons.example: a reader wanting a single revenue number for Johnson Plumbing is frustrated by a band tagged estimate-not-actual

failure_modes: letting a sub-category band attach to a named business as that business's revenue
stating a city/county figure or a supplier link without a source, derivation label, or inference flag
acceptance_tests: every dollar figure in any node is a labeled estimate or a cited public fact, no named-business actual revenue appears, each high-gross band carries its thin-net caveat, and coverage is stated as a floor
revisit_triggers: a new node introduces a dollar figure
a public-fact source is added or updated
an actual revenue datum becomes available to replace an estimate

base.update_signal: a new dollar figure is introduced or an actual datum becomes available

nodes.definition: Make the benchmark x size-signal method computationally explicit and auditable with a worked example, so the revenue bands are reproducible rather than asserted. The formula is firm_revenue_estimate = benchmark_per_unit x unit_count, where unit_count is read from an observable size signal and is itself UNKNOWN, producing a band rather than a point. Worked example for a multi-truck plumbing firm: a benchmark of 450000 dollars revenue per truck (midpoint of the 350k-550k/truck range) x 3 trucks (an inferred size signal) = 1350000 dollars, which sits inside the established multi-truck plumbing band of 800k-2.5M. The example recomputes correctly and demonstrates that the band is a transparent function of a published benchmark and an inferred unit count, never a stated fact about any named firm.

included: the firm_revenue_estimate = benchmark_per_unit x unit_count formula
excluded: the full per-sub-category band table (its own node)

pros.claim: A worked, recomputable formula makes the band method auditable and reproducible rather than asserted
pros.example: 450000 per truck x 3 trucks = 1350000 lets a reader verify the multi-truck plumbing band derivation end to end

cons.claim: The formula's unit_count input is an inferred size signal, so the output precision is illusory without measured counts
cons.example: if the firm actually runs 5 trucks not 3 the estimate is materially off

failure_modes: presenting the formula output as a measured revenue for a named firm
treating the inferred unit_count as known rather than a size-signal estimate
acceptance_tests: the formula firm_revenue_estimate = benchmark_per_unit x unit_count is stated, the worked example 450000 x 3 = 1350000 recomputes correctly and lands inside the stated multi-truck plumbing band, and the unit_count-is-inferred caveat is present
revisit_triggers: a benchmark-per-unit source updates
an observable unit count is measured for a firm
the per-sub-category band ranges are revised

base.update_signal: a benchmark-per-unit or measured unit-count changes

nodes.definition: Produce the market go/no-go verdict for adding a given trade or expanding a sub-category, composing the saturation read, the white-space rank, the growth/decline trajectory, the moat-vs-saturation split, and the regulatory cost gate into one decision. The merged rule: do not add a ninth commodity-mowing landscaper or a fourth residential cleaner into the price-competitive easy-entry tail (saturated/pressured, no moat); the genuinely under-served local opportunity sits in the licensed trades — above all electrical (solar/EV/panel), then commercial HVAC and premium landscape — where Modesto leakage and the licensing barrier have kept the local count thin and the moat protects whoever clears it. A demand-true opening that fails the CSLB/bond/WC/skilled-labor cost gate is a no-go until the gate clears; the succession-acquisition path is the alternative entry.

included: the cost-gate override and the succession alternative

pros.claim: Composing all reads into one verdict gives an actionable add/avoid call instead of scattered signals
pros.example: the verdict says no to a ninth landscaper but yes to a solar/EV electrical entrant once the C-10 gate is cleared

cons.claim: A single verdict can over-simplify a trade whose demand and licensing gate point opposite ways
cons.example: commercial HVAC has demand headroom yet still needs a C-20 holder and EPA-608 techs before a clean yes

failure_modes: issuing a yes on demand headroom while ignoring an unmet CSLB/skilled-labor gate
recommending a crowded easy-entry trade because local demand exists when pricing is a race to the bottom
acceptance_tests: the verdict for a proposed trade combines its saturation read, white-space rank, trajectory, moat status, and cost-gate status, names the do-not-add tail trades, and refuses any demand-true but cost-gated addition
revisit_triggers: a saturation read, trajectory, or cost gate feeding the verdict changes
a previously gated opening clears its cost gate
the SB 1455 WC shock lands and changes the licensed-entry calculus

base.update_signal: a saturation, trajectory, or cost-gate input to the verdict changes

nodes.definition: Define the loop that keeps the market reads current. A fixed refresh cadence (e.g., re-run on each major data release) plus material-change triggers — the SB 216 -> SB 1455 workers-comp-for-all-licensees deferral landing on 1/1/2028 (which raises the fixed-cost floor on the smallest licensed operators), a census/ACS demographic refresh, a solar/EV/panel adoption release, a major ag/food plant opening or closing, a building-permit-volume release, a CSLB licensing/fee change, or a firm opening/closing in the catalog — that send the analysis back through HOUSEHOLD_POOL and the saturation reads. Without this loop the 2026-06-30 snapshot silently goes stale as solar/EV demand rises, the aging housing stock keeps replacement demand steady, and Modesto's pull and the WC cost-shock move the equilibrium.

included: re-entry into pool sizing and saturation

pros.claim: A trigger list with the SB 1455 WC landing keeps the lowest-confidence reads on a path to refresh
pros.example: the WC-for-all deferral landing in 2028 fires the loop and re-tests the licensed-trade count

cons.claim: Too-frequent refresh churns the reads without new signal, since most inputs update only annually or on multi-year cycles
cons.example: re-sizing the household pool monthly when ACS counts move only yearly wastes effort

failure_modes: no cadence set so the snapshot ages silently past its trend and regulatory assumptions
ignoring a fired trigger (the WC shock landing) and continuing on a stale licensed-count read
acceptance_tests: a refresh cadence and an explicit material-change trigger list exist, each routing back to HOUSEHOLD_POOL and the saturation reads, with the SB 1455 WC landing named as a highest-leverage regulatory trigger
revisit_triggers: a material-change trigger fires
the cadence proves too frequent or too sparse for how the inputs actually update

base.update_signal: a material-change trigger fires or the cadence is tuned

edges.why_related: a high gross band tensions against the thin net reality, so gross can be misread as profit

edges.why_related: the verdict must read a thin cataloged count against the informal tail before calling true scarcity

conflict_axes.name: demand_headroom_vs_regulatory_gate
conflict_axes.description: A licensed trade can be demand-true white space yet be walled off by the CSLB license, $25k bond, WC and skilled-labor cost, so the demand and feasibility views point opposite ways.
poles: block on the unmet regulatory gate
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: treat a demand-true opening as a no-go until its CSLB/bond/WC/skilled-labor gate clears; demand never overrides licensing

conflict_axes.name: gross_revenue_vs_net_margin
conflict_axes.description: A high gross-revenue band (HVAC $1M-$3M) and a thin net margin (5-12%) describe the same firm, and reading gross as profit is the core misread.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: the gross band is the demand-size view; always pair it with the trade's net-margin caveat before any profit read

conflict_axes.name: catalog_floor_vs_true_density
conflict_axes.description: The 3.0/10k catalog density and the plausible 5-8/10k true density differ because the cash-basis informal tail is invisible, so a thin cataloged count may not be true scarcity.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: treat the catalog as a floor; read every thin sub-category as thin-among-cataloged-firms until a cash-economy survey confirms true scarcity

conflict_axes.name: licensing_moat_vs_easy_entry_saturation
conflict_axes.description: The licensing/skilled-labor barrier protects the thin licensed trades while its absence crowds the easy-entry tail, splitting the sector into a moat side and a saturation side.
poles: count is protected by the moat
count is crowded by easy entry
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: apply the moat read to electrical/HVAC/plumbing/flooring and the saturation read to janitorial/landscape maintenance; never read one engine's logic onto the other

conflict_axes.name: national_trend_vs_local_durability
conflict_axes.description: National decline signals (commodity landscape/cleaning pressure) can mislabel durable local incumbents with decades of contract retention.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: apply national pressure to undifferentiated easy-entry entrants; discount it for tenured incumbents (ASAP, Lopez) defended by contract retention

conflict_axes.name: annual_band_vs_seasonal_concentration
conflict_axes.description: A flat annual revenue band averages away the HVAC summer surge and landscape spring-fall peaks that drive working-capital risk.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: always pair the annual band with the trade's seasonal peak profile before any cash-flow read

conflict_axes.name: city_ceiling_vs_rural_trade_area
conflict_axes.description: Capping demand at the 73k city base understates the true addressable base because firms also draw from rural south Stanislaus County, an UNKNOWN uplift.
poles: cap demand at the city base
extend demand to the rural trade area
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: treat the city-only ceiling as conservative and flag the rural-county uplift as an UNKNOWN that makes the saturation read err toward under-counting demand

conflict_axes.name: estimate_labeling_vs_decisiveness
conflict_axes.description: Rigorous estimate-not-actual labeling protects honesty but can make the analysis read as too hedged to act on.
poles: label every figure as an estimate
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: label every figure but pair it with a confidence and a confirmation path so the read stays actionable without overclaiming a named-business revenue

conflict_axes.name: snapshot_stability_vs_trend_drift
conflict_axes.description: The ~22 equilibrium reads as stable, but rising solar/EV demand, Modesto's pull, and the SB 1455 WC cost-shock are moving the underlying forces.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: hold the snapshot as a dated baseline but let the review loop, not assumption, decide when drift has moved the equilibrium

edge_cases.description: A sub-category gross band is read as profit when the net margin is thin
edge_cases.trigger: a $1M-$3M HVAC gross band is quoted as if it were profit
edge_cases.mitigation: pair every gross band with its trade-specific net-margin reality (HVAC 5-12%, janitorial 10-25% on 50-60% labor) before any profit read

edge_cases.description: A sub-category band is attached to a named business as if it were that business's actual revenue
edge_cases.trigger: a per-sub-category estimate is quoted next to Johnson Plumbing or Saunders as fact
edge_cases.mitigation: keep every band sub-category-level and estimate-not-actual; never bind a dollar figure to a named business as fact

edge_cases.description: The 3.0/10k catalog density is read as true scarcity, missing the informal tail
edge_cases.trigger: the catalog floor is treated as the true operating count
edge_cases.mitigation: label 3.0/10k a floor, carry the 5-8/10k true-density estimate, and route to a cash-economy survey for confirmation

edge_cases.description: A licensed-trade white-space opening is recommended without pricing the CSLB/skilled-labor gate
edge_cases.trigger: electrical or HVAC is judged on demand headroom alone
edge_cases.mitigation: apply the CSLB license + $25k bond + WC + skilled-labor wall as an override before any licensed-trade yes

edge_cases.description: A C-20 HVAC entrant is assumed to claim a workers-comp exemption
edge_cases.trigger: an HVAC opening is costed without mandatory WC
edge_cases.mitigation: include mandatory WC for C-20 regardless of employee status and the SB 1455 WC-for-all landing in 2028 as binding cost

edge_cases.description: Commodity landscape maintenance is read as a growth lane because demand exists
edge_cases.trigger: local demand is conflated with a defensible, non-price-pressured opportunity
edge_cases.mitigation: classify commodity mowing as crowded, price-pressured and moat-less — pressured, not a growth lane

edge_cases.description: A strongly seasonal HVAC or landscape firm is sized on a flat annual band
edge_cases.trigger: an annual revenue band is used for cash-flow planning without the seasonal profile
edge_cases.mitigation: overlay the trade's peak profile (HVAC summer surge, landscape spring-fall) on the annual band before any working-capital read

edge_cases.description: The plumbing count is taken as 5 from the upstream analysis rather than the corrected 6
edge_cases.trigger: DeHart is netted out as HVAC instead of counted plumbing-primary
edge_cases.mitigation: use the reconciled 6 plumbing-primary count (DeHart is plumbing-primary with HVAC secondary); density on 22 total is unaffected

edge_cases.description: Turlock's count is read as a deficit by comparing raw firm numbers to larger Modesto
edge_cases.trigger: absolute firm counts are compared without normalizing per capita or accounting for leakage
edge_cases.mitigation: normalize to firms-per-10k and read the count as a Modesto-capped floor, not a deficit

edge_cases.description: HVAC capacity is read as 2 when functional capacity is ~4 with the plumbing cross-sellers
edge_cases.trigger: only the HVAC-primary count is used, ignoring DeHart and Turlock Plumbing H&A secondaries
edge_cases.mitigation: note the ~4 functional HVAC capacity from secondary-category tags; the thin label applies only to the headline primary count

edge_cases.description: The SB 1455 workers-comp deferral lands and raises the licensed-entry cost mid-snapshot
edge_cases.mitigation: fire the review loop, re-price the cost gate, and re-test whether the smallest licensed operators stay viable

workflow.description: Record the homeowner base, commercial/ag-facility accounts, and property-manager turns with cited magnitudes
workflow.gate: three buyer types each have a public-fact magnitude and a source confidence, and CSU students are excluded as high-ticket buyers

workflow.action: Tier demand by discretion and housing-stock driver
workflow.description: Split work into non-discretionary, recurring-contract and discretionary tiers and tie the aging-stock/climate replacement driver to it
workflow.gate: each discretion tier is named with a trade and its price sensitivity and out-of-pocket funding are stated

workflow.description: Derive ~23-25k households as 73k / ~2.9, with range, confidence, and the UNKNOWN rural-uplift caveat
workflow.gate: the pool is stated as an estimate-not-actual with derivation, range, and rural-uplift caveat

workflow.description: Derive each band as benchmark-per-unit x size signal with the unit-count-UNKNOWN caveat
workflow.gate: every band is estimate-not-actual with a size signal, confidence, and the unit-count-UNKNOWN caveat

workflow.action: Pair gross bands with net-margin reality
workflow.description: Attach each trade's net-margin range and labor-as-percent figure so gross is never read as profit
workflow.gate: each gross band carries a net-margin range and a labor-as-percent-of-revenue figure

workflow.action: Read the saturation equilibrium and two-speed barrier
workflow.description: Name the four forces holding the count at ~22 and the visible-floor-vs-true-count distinction
workflow.gate: all four forces are named and tied to the ~22-visible count with the floor-vs-true-count distinction

workflow.description: Set each sub-category catalog count against a crowded/moderate/thin read consistent with the barrier and leakage
workflow.gate: each of the six sub-categories has a count and a crowded/moderate/thin read, with the functional-vs-headline HVAC note

workflow.description: Classify trades as growing, stable or pressured and attach seasonality and the community labor base
workflow.gate: growing/stable/pressured lanes are named with their demand basis and seasonal peaks are flagged

workflow.action: Rank white-space and apply the regulatory gate
workflow.description: Order the defensible openings and mark each viable only after its CSLB/bond/WC/skilled-labor gate clears
workflow.gate: four+ openings are ranked, each with a demand basis and a cost/regulatory-gate qualifier, including the succession path

workflow.action: Contextualize against Modesto and the density floor
workflow.description: Compute the 3.0/10k floor against the national benchmark and read it with the Modesto leakage and informal tail
workflow.gate: the 3.0/10k floor, the 5-8/10k true density and the 15-25+/10k benchmark are stated with the artifact-vs-leakage read

workflow.action: Compose the market go/no-go verdict and review loop
workflow.description: Combine saturation, white-space, trajectory, moat and cost gate into an add/avoid call and set the refresh triggers
workflow.artifact: trade go/no-go verdict and review schedule
workflow.gate: the verdict refuses any demand-true but cost-gated addition, names the do-not-add tail trades, and a trigger list routes back to pool sizing and saturation

dominance_rules.rule: The revenue-honesty guardrail dominates any pressure for a single decisive number for a named business
dominance_rules.rationale: no per-business revenue is public for these privately held independents, so an over-decisive figure would be a fabrication
dominance_rules.trigger: a request for a named business's revenue or a single market number
dominance_rules.action: answer only with a labeled estimate (benchmark x size signal) plus confidence and confirmation path

dominance_rules.rule: The regulatory cost gate dominates a demand-true white-space opening
dominance_rules.rationale: CSLB licensing, the $25k bond, WC and skilled-labor scarcity can make a high-demand licensed trade un-enterable
dominance_rules.trigger: a white-space opening is judged attractive on demand alone
dominance_rules.action: mark it a no-go until the CSLB license, bond, WC and skilled-labor gate clears, or route to the succession-acquisition path

dominance_rules.rule: The net-margin reality dominates the gross-revenue band for any profit read
dominance_rules.rationale: a high gross band (HVAC $1M-$3M) is thin-net and not profit
dominance_rules.trigger: a gross band is used to characterize a trade's profitability
dominance_rules.action: pair it with the trade's net-margin range and labor-as-percent figure before any profit conclusion

dominance_rules.rule: Local-incumbent durability dominates national-decline signals for tenured easy-entry firms
dominance_rules.rationale: national commodity-cleaning or landscape pressure does not describe a 30-year contract-retained incumbent
dominance_rules.trigger: a national decline signal is applied to a tenured incumbent
dominance_rules.action: discount the national trend for firms with durable contract-retention moats (ASAP, Lopez)

dominance_rules.rule: The Modesto ceiling dominates demand math for high-ticket and specialty additions
dominance_rules.rationale: cross-shopping leaks high-ticket and specialty work to the larger neighbor regardless of local demand math
dominance_rules.trigger: a specialty or high-ticket addition is justified on Turlock demand alone
dominance_rules.action: cap the high-ticket addition at its Modesto-leakage-adjusted ceiling and prefer non-discretionary local-stays work

dominance_rules.rule: The seasonal profile dominates the annual band for cash-flow reads
dominance_rules.rationale: a flat annual band hides the HVAC summer surge and landscape spring-fall peaks that drive working-capital risk
dominance_rules.trigger: an annual band is used for a cash-flow or working-capital decision
dominance_rules.action: overlay the trade's seasonal peak profile before deciding

dominance_rules.rule: The catalog-is-a-floor rule dominates a thin-count scarcity conclusion
dominance_rules.rationale: the cash-basis informal tail is invisible, so a thin cataloged count may not be true scarcity
dominance_rules.trigger: a thin cataloged sub-category count is read as an open market
dominance_rules.action: read it as thin-among-cataloged-firms and adjust toward the 5-8/10k true-density estimate before calling scarcity

dominance_rules.rule: A flagged low-confidence input dominates a confident downstream conclusion built on it
dominance_rules.rationale: a conclusion cannot be more certain than its weakest load-bearing input
dominance_rules.trigger: the capture/density estimate or a benchmark band carries a conclusion above its own confidence
dominance_rules.action: cap the conclusion's confidence at that of its weakest input and name the confirmation source

dominance_rules.rule: Per-10k normalization dominates raw-count regional comparison
dominance_rules.rationale: comparing absolute firm counts across Turlock and a 3x-larger Modesto misleads
dominance_rules.trigger: Turlock's count is compared to Modesto without normalizing per capita or accounting for leakage
dominance_rules.action: convert to firms-per-10k and read the count as a Modesto-capped floor before drawing a saturation conclusion

anti_rework_rules.rule: Size the household pool before estimating per-sub-category bands or saturation
anti_rework_rules.prevents: deriving bands and saturation against a demand base that later moves, forcing a full re-derivation

anti_rework_rules.rule: Label every dollar figure estimate-not-actual at the moment it is written
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a later honesty sweep that must re-caveat figures already quoted as facts about a named firm

anti_rework_rules.rule: Pair every gross band with its net-margin reality when the band is built
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a profit conclusion drawn off a gross band that must be reworked once thin net margins surface

anti_rework_rules.rule: Apply the regulatory cost gate while ranking white-space, not after recommending it
anti_rework_rules.prevents: recommending a licensed-trade opening that the CSLB/bond/WC/skilled-labor gate then voids

anti_rework_rules.rule: Read saturation off the reconciled primary-category counts, noting HVAC secondaries, before tallying
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a plumbing-5 or HVAC-2 miscount that must be re-tallied against the reconciled 6 and functional ~4

anti_rework_rules.rule: Attach the seasonal profile to a trade's band when the band is built
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a flat-band cash-flow plan that must be reworked once the HVAC summer and landscape spring-fall peaks surface

anti_rework_rules.rule: Flag density as a floor and carry the informal-tail true-density estimate the first time it is used
anti_rework_rules.prevents: every downstream scarcity read inheriting an unflagged catalog count that must be re-marked

anti_rework_rules.rule: Name the confirmation path (CDTFA/licensing-board/permit-volume/cash-economy survey) on every low-confidence figure as it is stated
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a later pass to attach confirmation sources to numbers already published without them

anti_rework_rules.rule: Read demand against the city-ceiling-is-conservative rural-uplift caveat before calling a market saturated
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a saturated verdict drawn on the city base that must be revisited once rural-county draw is acknowledged

iteration_protocol.trigger: the SB 216 -> SB 1455 workers-comp-for-all-licensees deferral lands on 1/1/2028
iteration_protocol.action: re-price the regulatory cost gate and re-test whether the smallest licensed operators stay viable, re-issuing affected verdicts

iteration_protocol.trigger: a census/ACS demographic or household-count refresh lands
iteration_protocol.action: re-run the demand drivers and re-size the household pool

iteration_protocol.trigger: a solar/EV/panel-upgrade adoption release updates electrical demand
iteration_protocol.action: refresh the growth/decline trajectory and re-rank the electrical white-space

iteration_protocol.trigger: a major ag/food plant or distribution center opens or closes
iteration_protocol.action: update the commercial/ag-facility demand driver and re-read the affected saturation and white-space

iteration_protocol.trigger: a CSLB licensing, bond, or city/county permit fee changes
iteration_protocol.action: re-price the cost gate and re-issue any affected go/no-go verdicts

iteration_protocol.trigger: a firm opens or closes in the catalog
iteration_protocol.action: re-tally the saturation reads and the density floor

iteration_protocol.trigger: a building-permit-volume release quantifies replacement demand
iteration_protocol.action: re-derive the housing-stock driver and the affected benchmark bands

iteration_protocol.trigger: a cash-economy or informal-operator survey lands
iteration_protocol.action: re-derive the true-density estimate and re-read each thin sub-category against the tail

priority_rationale: Demand drivers, the discretion split and the housing-stock driver are foundational because pool sizing, saturation, bands and white-space all read from them; household-pool sizing precedes the per-sub-category bands and the margin reality they constrain; the saturation equilibrium, two-speed barrier, density floor and Modesto leakage build on the demand layer and feed the per-sub-category reads; seasonality/community, growth/decline, the informal tail, the regional context and the moat-vs-saturation read contextualize and overlay the saturation reads; the revenue-honesty guardrail and the worked benchmark formula govern every dollar expression; and the go/no-go verdict plus the review loop come last because they compose all upstream reads into a decision and a self-correcting refresh.
